I have the honor to report to the Committee on the outcome of the deliberations of the Working Group of the Whole of the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee held during the 69th Session of the committee. The working group was convened pursuant to the mandate agreed by the subcommittee at its 63rd session, as contained in the document A/AC.105/1346 and X1. In line with that mandate, the working group held a series of inter-sessional, informal, open-ended consultations in March, April, and May this year. Followed by two formal meetings during this session of the Committee to address the effects of the liquidity situation and to improve the organization and working methods of the Committee and its subsidiary bodies. In the course of the informal consultations, the Working Group focused on matters requiring immediate attention, namely the continuity of the provision of United Nations Web TV for meetings of the Committee and its subcommittees,: the possible merging of agenda items across the three bodies; the structure of reports; and guidance to the Secretariat in relation to the organization of sessions in the context of the ongoing liquidity situation. On the structure of reports, while no consensus was reached on all aspects, there is a common understanding within the Working Group that the reports should include a procedural section and a section on decisions and recommendations. Further work will be required to achieve convergence on appropriate— on approaches to reflecting views expressed by the delegations and discussions held. At the same time, the work undertaken by the working group has enabled delegations to better understand the range of options available, thereby hopefully creating a more solid basis for achieving convergence during the adoption of the report of the committee at the present session. Regarding the guidance to the Secretariat in the context of liquidity constraints, delegations expressed differing views on possible adjustments to the duration and organization of sessions, including whether sessions could be shortened or maintained in their current format. On WebTV, deliberations demonstrated convergence towards provisional agreement— arrangement— agreement that regular budget-mandated meetings of the the Committee and its subcommittees should continue to be webcast on United Nations Web TV, including through arrangements whereby the associated costs may be covered by the Office for Outer Space Affairs. Such arrangements could be made, for example, through voluntary cash contributions and on the understanding that no resources allocated for capacity-building activities should be used to cover the cost of Web TV. Turning to the issue related to the agenda, the Working Group also demonstrated convergence towards a provisional agreement that proposals for the inclusion of new items on the agenda of the Committee or its subcommittees should be accompanied by clearly defined objectives, expected outputs or deliverables, and an indicative timeframe for consideration of the proposed item. There was also broad provisional support for amendments to the agenda of the Committee starting from its 70th session in 2027. The amendments include the merger of the items on space and water and space and climate change into an item entitled Space for Water and Climate, as well as the merger of the items on spin-off benefits of space technology, review of current status, and space exploration and innovation into an item entitled Space Exploration, Innovation, and Spin-off Benefits of Space Technology. Furthermore, the Working Group also positively considered, on a provisional basis, modifications to the agenda of the Legal Subcommittee starting from its 66th session in 2027 through the merger of the items on Status and Application of the Five United Nations Treaties on Outer Space and Ways and Means, including capacity building to promote their implementation, and general exchange of information on non-legally binding United Nations instruments on outer space into an item entitled Status and Application of the Five United Nations Treaties on Outer Space and Ways and Means, including capacity building to enhance the implementation of United Nations instruments relevant to international space law. Finally, there was an understanding within the working group that matters identified at the 63rd session of the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, raised by delegations during the intersessional period as well as at the present session, together with any other issues that delegations may wish to raise, will continue to be considered by the working group at its next session in 2027. Mr. Chair, The work of the Working Group of the Whole has made a substantial and constructive contribution to the further improvement of the Committee's work. Through sustained engagement, delegations have been able to achieve considerable progress in identifying practical and forward-looking solutions on the complex and cross-cutting issues outlined above. The outlines of the Working Group are now submitted to the Committee for its consideration under the relevant agenda item. Distinguished delegates, ladies, gentlemen, it's an honor to represent Italian Space Agency here at COPOS 2026. Our journey today starts with a brief look at the global nanosatellite sector, followed by an in-depth view of the Italian Alcor program and 4 of its flagship missions: PIS, PQIoT, EarthNext, and SATURN. Nowadays, The micro and nano satellite missions are a well-established sector all over the world, and the landscape is expanding rapidly. Currently, the United States leads with 56% of launches, followed by Europe at 16.2%, Russia at 7%, and many other nations more and more interested in these type of missions. While these missions are historically driven by university, now we see a massive shift toward commercial companies, which account for nearly 60% of all launched nanosatellites, and space agencies are increasingly playing a pivotal role in transitioning these platforms from educational tools to robust in-orbit demonstrators. But what is clearly seen by this graph is that with the passing years, there is almost an exponential growth of microsatellite missions, possibly making of them a solid space infrastructure for the future services. ASIS' response to this trend is the Alcor program. This initiative is designed to foster space diplomacy and international collaboration while supporting vibrant national ecosystems of over 100 small and medium enterprises, research centers, and universities, with a selection criteria always based on innovation, strategy, and feasibility. Through a rigorous selection process, 20 innovative proposals were chosen based on their strategy, innovation, and feasibility to demonstrate new enabling technologies in orbit spanning from telecom, in-space navigation, up to Earth observation, to the IoT and space exploration. But today, as I said, we will focus on 4 of them: 2 IoT missions, Pico IoT and BIS, and 2 Earth observation missions, which are EarthNext and SATURN. Our first highlighted mission is BIS. Which stands for Bidirectional IoT Satellite Service. This is an agile 6U platform operating at 500 km low Earth orbit. The key concept here is the transition from localized networks to a seamless low-power global area network, LPGAN. Unlike traditional systems, this enables true bidirectional communication, allowing operator not only to receive data but also to send active commands to remote off-grid assets. With an expected launch in Q3 2027, PEACE will provide low-cost accessibility for non-governmental organizations and developing regions previously priced out of orbital connectivity. And already now, before the demonstration mission has started, there are national stakeholders which are interested in buying this service, and we are already discussing with them to understand how to provide this kind of services. Parallel to this, the PICO-IoT mission pushes the boundaries of miniaturization to support Sustainable Development Goal 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure. This constellation consists of 3 0.3u PICO satellites with a tiny dimension of 3 by 10 by 10 centimeters. Centimeters and weighing only approximately 0.5 kilograms each. The mission will demonstrate handling of non-time-latency-tolerant IoT packets and prioritizing data management. The most important packets are delivered first. A major innovation here is also the ADARD system, Aerodynamic Drag Aided Rapid Deployment, which supports the rapid decay of the orbit. Thus freeing the orbital space in line with sustainability development goals. As you can see here, PIS and PIC-IoT are specifically designed for resilient application in smart agriculture, infrastructure, and environmental monitoring, providing near real-time data retrieval in areas where terrestrial infrastructure is entirely lacking or anyhow not easy to build. Moving on Earth observation, EarthNext represents a breakthrough in very low Earth orbit operations. Operating at just 300 km, this 16U CubeSat utilizes the Regulus compact electric thruster to compensate for atmospheric drag. This low altitude allows for higher resolution multispectral imaging with a ground sampling distance of 2.5 up to 12 meters. Most importantly for this forum, EarthNext promotes sustainable space management. At 300 kilometers, in fact, the atmosphere acts as a natural cleaner, ensuring rapid orbital decay at the end of the mission and achieving zero long-term debris. The launch of the satellite and the beginning of the mission is scheduled for Q1 2029. Finally, we have SATURN, a mission focused on swarm-based active SAR, a Synthetic Aperture Radar, with a MIMO acquisition architecture which allows resolution even with small satellites. For the ones that do not know, a MIMO architecture is a type of mission where multiple radars send a signal to the Earth which is then retrieved by all of the, all of the satellites which are in orbit, allowing a more and more accurate ground sampling distance. SATURN uses a coordinated swarm of 16 U maintaining a strict 200-meter relative distance, unified by intersatellite links which allow the communication among the satellites. We expect SATURN to be launched in Q4 2028. These resilience escalator architectures allows therefore for a scalable constellation capable of an ultra-low 1.5-hour revisit time. This mission is critical for on-demand disaster assessment, providing all-weather, day and night imaging for maritime monitoring and rapid response to floods or landslides. From Earth observation to space weather and global connectivity, therefore, these missions demonstrate Italy's commitment to a multidisciplinary and sustainable approach to space. And through the Alcor program, ASI is not just sending satellites or launching satellites, we are building a global infrastructure for a more resilient future. Thank you very much.
